title: Compliance and the Deterrence of Checking
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that the strongest deterrent against rule-breaking isn't the severity of punishment but the visible presence of a monitoring system. Leaders face a balancing act: too little oversight invites violations, while too much explicit talk about compliance can feel like a straitjacket that stifles trust and creativity. Drawing on research showing regular checks outperform harsh penalties as deterrents, the author recommends embedding compliance quietly into everyday processes rather than constantly announcing it. The Bill Russell quote about the threat of a blocked shot mattering as much as the block itself anchors the argument.
points: The mere expectation of being checked deters rule-breaking more than the severity of punishment does
Overemphasizing compliance can stifle creativity, experimentation, and trust on a team
Best practice: embed compliance into normal processes rather than constantly broadcasting the rules
A visible, consistent monitoring system builds a stable, ethical organization without heavy-handed reminders
quotes: Sometimes, even a minor violation can impact the integrity, safety, and legal standing of the organization.
The mere possibility and expectation of compliance checks act as a deterrent to rule-breaking behavior.
Research has consistently shown that random or regular monitoring is a stronger deterrent than the severity of whatever the punishment might be.
The simple existence of a system acts as a deterrence against rule-breaking and cutting corners.
The idea is not to block every shot. The idea is to make your opponent believe that you might block every shot.
